title: Design a Distributed Job Scheduler (Cron at Scale)
prompt: Design a distributed job scheduler: users register one-off and recurring (cron-style) jobs that must fire at or near their scheduled time and run to completion exactly the intended number of times, across a fleet of workers. Cover how you store schedules, trigger them on time, and execute them reliably.
blurb: The scheduling-at-scale problem — time-based indexing (time-wheel/bucketed queues), dedup so a job fires once, and at-least-once execution with idempotent workers.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (register one-off/recurring jobs, cancel, retries, cron semantics) from non-functional (fire within tolerance, no missed jobs, no unbounded duplicates, durability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about number of jobs, firing granularity/tolerance, exactly-once vs at-least-once, max concurrency, timezone/DST handling, retry policy.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Derives jobs due per second at peak, storage for schedules, worker fleet sizing, and queue throughput.

rubric.label: Time indexing / trigger mechanism
rubric.description: How due jobs are found on time: time-wheel, bucketed 'due at' index, DB polling with a time index, or delay queue — and the tradeoffs of each at scale.

rubric.label: Delivery semantics
rubric.description: Why exactly-once firing is hard; settle on at-least-once + idempotent execution with dedup keys; how retries interact with duplicates.

rubric.label: Dedup & coordination
rubric.description: Ensuring one dispatcher claims a due job (locks/leases/leader election/partitioning) so it isn't triggered by multiple nodes simultaneously.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Schedule store -> dispatcher(s) scanning due jobs -> queue -> worker pool -> execution/result store; recurrence recomputes next fire time.

rubric.label: Reliability & failure handling
rubric.description: Dispatcher crash mid-scan, worker crash mid-job, clock skew, catch-up after downtime, missed-fire policy.

rubric.label: Scaling
rubric.description: Partition schedules by time bucket / job id, multiple dispatchers without double-firing, backpressure when due jobs spike.

rubric.label: Bottlenecks
rubric.description: Thundering herd at round times (e.g., every job at :00), hot time buckets, dispatcher as SPOF, long-running jobs starving workers.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Fire-time skew (scheduled vs actual), execution success/retry rates, queue depth, missed/late-job alerts.

functional_requirements: Register one-off jobs (run at time T)
Cancel or update a scheduled job
Execute the job's action (callback/HTTP/enqueue) with retries
nonfunctional_requirements: Jobs fire within a bounded tolerance of their target time
No silently missed jobs; durable schedules
Survives dispatcher/worker crashes and short outages (catch-up)
clarifying_questions: How many active scheduled jobs, and how many due per second at peak?
What firing precision/tolerance is acceptable (seconds? sub-second?)
Do we need exactly-once, or is at-least-once + idempotency acceptable?
Max concurrent executions and per-job timeout?
How are timezones/DST and cron ambiguities handled?
Retry/backoff policy and dead-letter behavior on repeated failure?
qualifying_questions: After an outage, do we run all missed fires, the latest only, or skip?
Are job actions idempotent, or must the scheduler guarantee single delivery?
Is fairness across tenants required (no one tenant starves others)?

estimations.traffic: 100M scheduled jobs; if evenly spread, thousands due/sec, but real load spikes at round times (:00, midnight). Design for the peak bucket, not the average.
estimations.storage: 100M jobs x ~1KB (cron spec, payload, next_fire, state) ~= 100GB in a partitioned store.
estimations.workers: If avg job runs 200ms and peak is 20K due/sec, need ~4K concurrent worker slots; long jobs need isolation to avoid head-of-line blocking.
estimations.granularity: Bucket the timeline into 1s (or coarser) slots; a due-scan runs each tick.

core_components: Durable schedule store (partitioned by time bucket)
data_model: jobs(job_id PK, owner, action, cron|run_at, next_fire_at, status, timezone, retry_policy)
due_index(bucket_ts, job_id) — time-partitioned index of what fires when
executions(job_id, fire_ts, attempt, status, worker_id) — dedup + audit
api_design: POST /jobs { action, schedule (cron|at), payload, retry_policy } -> job_id
reference.high_level_design: Schedules live in a durable store, indexed by a 'next_fire_at' time bucket so due jobs are cheap to find. Dispatchers own disjoint partitions of the timeline (via leases / leader election / consistent-hash of buckets) and, each tick, claim jobs whose next_fire_at <= now, write an execution row keyed by (job_id, fire_ts) for dedup, enqueue a task, and — for recurring jobs — compute the next fire time and reschedule. Workers pull from the queue, execute idempotently (guarded by the (job_id, fire_ts) key), and record results; failures retry with backoff and eventually dead-letter. Firing is at-least-once; correctness comes from idempotent execution plus the dedup key, not from trying to make delivery exactly-once.

deep_dives.probe: How do you find the jobs due right now without scanning 100M rows every second — time-wheel, bucketed due-index, delay queue, or DB polling on a time index? Tradeoffs?
Can you guarantee a job fires exactly once? If not, why, and how do you make at-least-once safe — dedup keys, idempotent workers, fencing?
Two dispatchers scan the same bucket. How do you ensure a due job is claimed and enqueued by exactly one — leases, partition ownership, conditional writes?
Half your jobs are 'daily at midnight'. How do you avoid a giant spike at :00 — jitter, spreading, sharded buckets, rate-limited draining?
A dispatcher was down for 10 minutes. On recovery, thousands of jobs are overdue. Do you run them all, coalesce to the latest, or skip — and how does the policy get expressed per job?

Job definitions and execution results live in a datastore. How do you stream state changes (created/updated/fired) to an audit log, search index, or analytics pipeline — change data capture / Debezium off the store, or explicit event emission?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions queue or kafka or sqs
followup_bank.question: Does the queue give at-least-once or exactly-once, and how do visibility timeouts / redelivery interact with your dedup key?
If you cache the due-index or use Redis for the time-wheel, what is the eviction/expiry policy and how do you avoid a stampede when a hot time bucket's entries all come due at once?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions database or postgres or sql or dynamo
followup_bank.question: How do you stream job/execution state changes to audit and analytics — CDC/Debezium off the store vs dual writes? And how do you index next_fire_at for cheap due-scans?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions lock or lease or leader
followup_bank.question: How do you handle a dispatcher that holds a lease but is partitioned/GC-paused — fencing tokens so a stale owner can't double-dispatch?
Where is the dedup key stored, and what is its lifetime so retries within a window are deduped but the same job can fire again next period?

scaling: Partition the timeline/jobs across dispatchers via consistent hashing or leased partitions
Bucket due-index by second/minute to bound scan size
Add jitter and spread to flatten round-time spikes
Isolate long-running jobs on separate worker pools to avoid head-of-line blocking
Per-tenant rate limits and fair queuing
bottlenecks: Thundering herd at round times (:00, midnight)
Dispatcher as a single point of failure per partition
Dedup store write rate at peak
tradeoffs: At-least-once + idempotency (practical) vs exactly-once (usually impossible end-to-end)
DB polling (simple, load) vs time-wheel/delay-queue (efficient, more moving parts)
Fine granularity (precise, costly) vs coarse buckets (cheap, jitter)
Run-all missed vs coalesce-latest after downtime
alternative_solutions: DB with a next_fire_at index + polling dispatchers (Quartz-style)
Hashed/hierarchical time-wheel in memory backed by durable store
Delay queues (SQS delay / Redis sorted-set by fire time / Kafka + tumbling)
Cloud-native (per-job cloud timers) for lower scale
observability: Fire-time skew: scheduled vs actual firing time
Execution success, retry, and dead-letter rates
Dispatcher lease churn / partition rebalance events
security: Authn/authz on job registration; per-tenant isolation
Validate/sandbox job actions (SSRF on HTTP callbacks, resource limits)
Rate-limit job creation and per-tenant concurrency caps
Audit trail of who scheduled/changed what
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer scopes firing tolerance and delivery semantics up front, then indexes schedules by next_fire_at (time-wheel or bucketed due-index) so due-scans are cheap. Dispatchers own disjoint timeline partitions via leases/leader election and use conditional writes plus an (job_id, fire_ts) dedup key so a job is enqueued once; execution is at-least-once with idempotent workers and retries/dead-letter. It handles the round-time thundering herd with jitter/spreading, defines a catch-up policy after outages, uses fencing tokens against stale lease holders, and streams job/execution state to audit/analytics via CDC. It names the thundering herd and long-job head-of-line blocking as the key bottlenecks.

interviewer_notes: The two make-or-break areas are (1) how due jobs are found on time — push for a time-wheel or bucketed due-index rather than 'scan the table every second' — and (2) delivery semantics, where a senior candidate concedes exactly-once is impractical and builds at-least-once + idempotency with a dedup key. Probe coordination: how two dispatchers avoid double-firing (leases/partitions/fencing). If they add a datastore, hit the CDC/Debezium probe; if they add Redis/cache for the time-wheel, probe expiry and hot-bucket stampede. Save time for the round-time thundering herd and the post-outage catch-up policy.
